segments.say: Lesson 5. Hash Maps & Sets. How a dict finds anything instantly (hashing explained), then the "have I seen this?", counting and grouping patterns, with Two Sum.

A hash map (Python dict ) stores key leads to value pairs and finds any key almost instantly, no matter how many items it holds. A hash set ( set ) stores just keys. Here is an analogy. A cloakroom: you hand over your coat and get ticket number 47. Later you show number 47 and the attendant goes straight to hook 47. No searching through every coat.

Why does this matter? It's the number 1 tool for turning an O of n squared "search for a matching element" into O of n. Used for counting, grouping, de-duplicating and "have I seen this before?". A few key words. Key: What you look up by (a name, a number, a tuple). Value: What's stored for that key. Hash function: Turns a key into a bucket number. Bucket: A slot in the underlying array. Collision: Two keys landing in the same bucket. Complement: The other number you need: target minus x.

segments.say: Lookup d "apple": compute the hash again, giving 3 leads to jump straight there. No scanning, so O of 1 on average.

segments.sec: Watch: How a hash map finds things instantly
segments.say: A collision: "plum" also lands in 3. The bucket keeps a small chain of both pairs. Python resizes the table to keep chains short, so lookups stay ~ O of 1.

segments.say: A set is the same thing with keys only. Perfect for "have I seen this before?" in O of 1.

The pattern. Whenever brute force asks "does some earlier element satisfy X?", replace the inner loop with a hash map / set lookup. Typical uses:. Complement lookup: Two Sum (target minus x). Counting / frequency: Counter for anagrams, majority element, top-k. Grouping by a canonical key: sorted letters for anagrams. Existence / dedupe: set for "contains duplicate", longest consecutive sequence.

Signals in the problem statement. "Find a pair / complement", "first unique", "count occurrences", "group by", "anagram", "duplicate". Unsorted input where sorting would cost O of n log n or destroy indices.
Template. Here is the code. Pause the video to read it line by line.
Gotchas. Insert after checking, so an element doesn't pair with itself. Lists aren't hashable. Use a tuple as the key. Hash ops are O of 1 average; mention it.

Problem 1: Two Sum. Given a list of numbers nums and a number target, return the indexes of the two numbers that add up to target. Exactly one answer exists, and you can't use the same element twice. For example, with nums equals 2, 7, 11, 15, target equals 9, the answer is 0, 1. nums index 0 plus nums index 1 equals 2 plus 7 equals 9
What is it really asking? For each number x, the partner you need is target minus x (its "complement"). The question becomes: have I already seen the complement?

The obvious brute force: Check every pair with two nested loops: for i, for j greater than i, if nums index i plus nums index j equals target return i, j. That costs O of n squared time, O of 1 space. The smart way: One pass with a dict of value leads to index; check for the complement before inserting. Step by step: Create an empty dict seen mapping value leads to index. Then, For each index i with value x, compute need equals target minus x. Then, If need is in seen, return seen index need, i. Then, Otherwise store seen index x equals i and continue.
Here is the Python solution. Complexity: O of n time, O of n space. Pause and read through it, then try writing it yourself without looking.

Problem 2: Group Anagrams. Given a list of words, group together the words that are anagrams of each other (same letters, different order). Return the groups in any order. For example, with "eat","tea","tan","ate","nat","bat", the answer is "eat","tea","ate", "tan","nat", "bat". "eat", "tea" and "ate" all use the letters a, e, t

The obvious brute force: For every word, compare it with every other word (sorting both to check anagram-ness). That costs O of n squared, k log k time. The smart way: Anagrams share the same sorted letters (or the same 26-letter count). Use that as the dict key. Step by step: For each word, compute a key that's identical for anagrams: tuple(sorted(word)). Then, Append the word to groups index key (a defaultdict(list)). Then, Return all the dict's values.
Here is the Python solution. Complexity: O of n, k log k time, O of n, k space. Pause and read through it, then try writing it yourself without looking.

Problem 3: Longest Consecutive Sequence. Given an unsorted list of integers, return the length of the longest run of consecutive numbers (like 1, 2, 3, 4). Must run in O of n. For example, with nums equals 100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2, the answer is 4. 1, 2, 3, 4 are all present

The obvious brute force: Sort, then scan for runs. Simple, but O of n log n, which breaks the O of n requirement. Even slower: for each number, keep checking x+1, x+2. with a list search. That costs O of n log n or O of n cubed. The smart way: Put everything in a set. Only start counting from numbers that begin a run (x minus 1 not in set), so each number is visited at most twice. Step by step: Put all numbers in a set for O of 1 lookups. Then, For each x, only start counting if x minus 1 is N O T in the set (x is the start of a run). Then, Count upward while x+1, x+2. are in the set. Then, Track the longest run.
Here is the Python solution. Complexity: O of n time, O of n space. Pause and read through it, then try writing it yourself without looking.

A likely interview question: When do you reach for a hash map? A strong answer: When brute force repeatedly searches earlier elements: complements, counts, grouping, seen-before checks. It trades O of n space for O of 1 average lookups, turning O of n squared into O of n.
